title: Progressive's Second-Quarter Premiums Rose 5% to $21.1 Billion and Net Income Hit $3.31 Billion, but June's Combined Ratio Slipped to 90.0
summary: Progressive's second-quarter 2026 net premiums written rose 5% to $21.08 billion and net income reached $3.31 billion, but its June combined ratio worsened to 90.0 from 86.6 and June net income fell 31% to $779 million as policies in force reached 40.09 million.
description:
Progressive's second-quarter 2026 results gave a mixed picture of the US auto insurance market: more customers and higher premiums, but a combined ratio that moved the wrong way in the final month of the quarter. Because Progressive reports monthly as well as quarterly, and is the largest writer of personal auto insurance in the United States, its numbers are watched as an early indicator for competitors. The figures below come from Insurance Business US, which reported them on July 16, 2026. Progressive later reported its third-quarter results, covered separately on this site, so this article should be read as a record of the second quarter.

Premiums and earnings

Net premiums written, the premium the company keeps after reinsurance, rose 5% in the quarter to $21.08 billion. Net premiums earned, the portion recognised as revenue as policy periods pass, rose 6% to $21.57 billion. For the first half of the year, net premiums written were $44.69 billion. Net income for the quarter was $3.31 billion, up 4%, and for the first half it was $6.13 billion. The quarterly profit included $604 million of realized investment gains, which means the underwriting and investment income alone did not account for the full amount. Readers comparing Progressive with competitors should remember that realized gains can vary from quarter to quarter.

The combined ratio

The combined ratio is claims and expenses as a percentage of premiums earned, and a ratio below 100 indicates an underwriting profit. Progressive's was 87.3 for the second quarter, compared with 86.2 a year earlier, which means slightly less underwriting profit per dollar of premium. For the year to date the ratio was 86.9. Progressive sets a goal of keeping the combined ratio below 96, so all of these figures sit well inside its own target, and by a considerable margin.

June was weaker. The one-month combined ratio was 90.0, up from 86.6 in June of the previous year, and June net income fell 31% to $779 million. The monthly numbers can swing more sharply than the quarterly ones because of timing of claims and of catastrophe losses, so a single month does not establish a trend. However, the direction, a higher combined ratio and falling income in the final month of the quarter, shows why analysts follow the monthly releases closely. The source does not break down the cause of the June change, and this article does not speculate about it.

Policy growth

Policies in force reached 40.09 million, up 7%. Of those, personal lines policies totalled 38.86 million, up 8%. Within personal lines, direct auto, meaning policies sold directly to consumers through Progressive's own channels, rose 10% to 16.72 million, while agency auto, sold through independent agents, rose 8% to 11.21 million. Special lines, which include motorcycles, boats and recreational vehicles, accounted for 7.30 million policies. Property policies were 3.63 million, up 1%, and commercial lines policies were 1.23 million.

The faster growth in direct auto than in agency auto is consistent with Progressive's long-standing emphasis on direct sales. Property growth of 1% is small compared with auto.

What the numbers suggest

Taken together, the figures describe an insurer that is still growing its customer base strongly while earning healthy margins, but whose profitability per policy is easing a little. Premium growth of 5% is much slower than policy growth of 7%, which implies that the average premium per policy is not rising as fast as customer numbers. That is arithmetic from the two reported growth rates and not a company statement, which is consistent with, though not proof of, a cooling in price increases.

For drivers, a softening market can mean more competition for their business and, in some states, slower increases or even reductions at renewal. For investors, the question is whether growth can continue without eroding margins, since insurers often chase market share when prices are high and profits are strong. For regulators, the monthly data provide an early check on whether rate filings match emerging loss experience.

What the numbers do not show

Several things cannot be read from the Insurance Business summary. It does not give the claims frequency or severity trends that sit behind the combined ratio, it does not report the effect of catastrophe losses in the quarter, and it does not break out how much of the premium growth came from rate changes and how much from additional policies. It also does not compare Progressive with competitors. Analysts who want to understand why June was weaker than the quarter as a whole would need the company's detailed monthly release and the commentary on its investor call. A combined ratio of 90.0 in a single month remains profitable underwriting by the company's own standards, since its goal is anything below 96, and the same is true of the 87.3 for the quarter. The point for readers is the change in direction in one month, not an alarming level.

The monthly reporting rhythm itself is part of the story. Progressive publishes results every month, which gives investors and rivals a regular view of how pricing, claims and growth are moving. The July 16 report is the latest in that sequence.

Looking ahead

The company scheduled its quarterly investor call for August 4. Progressive's subsequent monthly and quarterly reports, including the third-quarter results published in October, show how the trends developed, and readers should consult those and the company's filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission for the latest numbers.

This article summarises a trade-press report of company-published figures. It is general information and not investment advice.

key_points: Second-quarter net premiums written rose 5% to $21.08 billion and net premiums earned rose 6% to $21.57 billion; first-half net premiums written were $44.69 billion.
The June combined ratio was 90.0 against 86.6 a year earlier, the second-quarter ratio was 87.3 against 86.2, and the year-to-date ratio was 86.9, within the company's goal of below 96.
Second-quarter net income was $3.31 billion, up 4%, including $604 million of realized gains, while June net income fell 31% to $779 million; first-half net income was $6.13 billion.
Policies in force reached 40.09 million, up 7%, including 38.86 million personal lines policies, up 8%, and 16.72 million direct auto policies, up 10%.
Property policies in force were 3.63 million, up 1%, and commercial policies were 1.23 million; the company's investor call for the quarter was set for August 4.
why_it_matters: Progressive is the largest US writer of personal auto insurance and reports monthly, so its figures are an early read on the whole market. Growth in policies with a rising combined ratio suggests the cycle is turning from rapid rate increases toward competition for customers, which affects what drivers pay.

title: FCA Launches a £2 Million 'You Don't Need to Pay to Claim' Car Finance Campaign as 27% of Consumers Say They Lack Confidence to Complain Alone
summary: The Financial Conduct Authority's £2 million campaign, running from July 27 to September 6, 2026 across TV, radio, print, billboards and social media, tells motor finance customers they can complain for free, citing research that 27% lack the confidence to complain without a claims firm or law firm.
description:
The Financial Conduct Authority has put money and media behind a simple message to people who bought a car on finance: you don't need to pay to claim. The regulator's campaign, which it says is backed by £2 million, runs from July 27 to September 6, 2026 and uses television, radio, print, billboards and social media. It is aimed at motor finance customers who may be owed compensation under the redress scheme the FCA put in place after years of scrutiny of historic commission arrangements between lenders and car dealers. The information below comes from the FCA's own press release, which gives both the campaign details and the research that prompted it. Dates on the page differ slightly, with the release showing a first-published date of July 27 and the page metadata showing July 23, so readers should check the FCA site for the current version.

The message and the research behind it

The central message is that consumers can complain directly to their lender for free and, if they are unhappy with the outcome, take the matter to the Financial Ombudsman Service, also free, without involving a claims management company or a law firm that might charge a fee. The FCA's concern is that fees reduce the amount consumers keep. It had earlier run a first phase of the campaign, reported by Legal Futures on September 15, 2025, which cost £1 million and warned that people using a claims firm could lose over 30% of their compensation. The latest phase doubles the spend.

To judge whether the message was reaching people, the FCA commissioned a Kantar survey of 1,000 people, conducted from June 25 to 28, 2026. The results are the most useful part of the release. Some 27% of respondents said they lack the confidence to complain without the help of a claims management company or law firm. Some 59% said they had made a claim or were considering one, and 23% were unsure. These figures describe a population that is engaged with the issue but not certain about how to proceed, which is the situation in which a paid intermediary can seem attractive.

The FCA responded with a practical tool: a free template complaint letter. According to the release, more than 80% of the survey respondents said the template would make them more confident about complaining directly. The regulator did not say in the release how many people have downloaded or used the template, so its real-world effect cannot be assessed from this source.

Reach so far

The FCA also gave figures for the campaign's reach. It said video on demand had generated about 11 million views, that there had been 2,180 outdoor placements, and that print circulation was close to 3 million. These are regulator-reported delivery figures. They show how widely the material was distributed, not how many consumers changed their behaviour, and the release does not say whether claims to lenders or to claims firms have fallen as a result.

Sheree Howard of the FCA is quoted in the release on the regulator's concern that people should not pay unnecessarily. The release makes clear that the campaign sits alongside the redress scheme itself, which the FCA launched in March 2026. It puts the scheme's value at £7.5 billion, and it describes the scheme as currently partially suspended. The release does not give the reasons for the suspension in the part reviewed for this article, and readers should consult the FCA's scheme pages for the current position on timing and eligibility.

Why intermediaries matter in redress

When a large redress exercise is announced, claims management companies and law firms typically advertise heavily, often offering to handle the process for a percentage of the compensation. Some people value that service, particularly if they have lost paperwork or find the process daunting. The FCA's position, however, is that the scheme is designed so that consumers can claim without paying. By publicising the free routes, it is trying to ensure that the money intended for consumers goes to them. The 30% figure from the earlier phase illustrates why this matters: on a payout of several hundred pounds, a fee of that size can make a material difference to a household.

The campaign is also a response to the information gap that follows a complex regulatory decision. Many people do not know that they took out a loan with a discretionary commission arrangement, or that a complaint can be made without legal representation. The survey suggests that even among those who know the facts, confidence can be low. The template letter and the broad-based advertising are attempts to address both.

What consumers can do

Consumers who think they were affected should start by checking their finance agreements and contacting the lender directly, using the template or their own wording. If the lender rejects the complaint or does not respond in time, the Financial Ombudsman Service can review it at no cost. Anyone who decides to use a claims firm or a law firm should ask in advance what it will charge and how that compares with the expected compensation, and should keep copies of all correspondence. The FCA's website carries its guidance and the template.

The campaign will run until September 6. Whether it reduces use of paid intermediaries will become clear only when the FCA, lenders and the ombudsman publish data on complaint volumes and on how claims were submitted. This article summarises a regulator's press release and a survey it commissioned, and is general information and not legal or financial advice.

A Kantar survey of 1,000 people on June 25 to 28 found that 27% lack confidence to complain without a claims management company or law firm, 59% have made or are considering a claim and 23% are unsure.

The FCA reported about 11 million video-on-demand views, 2,180 outdoor placements and print circulation near 3 million, and offers a free template complaint letter that over 80% of those surveyed said would make them more confident.
The redress scheme, launched in March and put at £7.5 billion, is described as currently partially suspended.
An earlier £1 million phase in September 2025 warned that using a claims firm could cost consumers over 30% of their compensation.
why_it_matters: Every pound a motor finance customer pays to a claims firm or law firm comes out of their compensation, so the regulator is trying to move people toward a free route. The survey result that more than a quarter feel unable to complain alone suggests the campaign is aimed at a confidence gap, not only an information gap.
